# Higher Education During the 20th Century: The Birth of College Majors

Heather Huntington

Heather Huntington

2021, Academia Letters

Abstract

At the beginning of the 20th century, the elective system, lacking any prescribed curricular path, began to break down. Within a few years, many of the colleges changed to "concentration and distribution" general education requirements. Curriculum committees were created to negotiate the curriculum changes, and it was usually the concentration that benefited. Thus, college "majors" were born. A Shift from the Elective System Toward a Major Concentration and Distribution Requirements At the beginning of the 20th century, it was becoming more common for young people to finish high school and move on to college. The initiation of American graduate schools in the 1890s also created an oversupply of Ph.D.s. This ultimately led to the availability of more qualified teachers for the higher education revolution of the 20th century, where many higher educational institutions changed to an elective curriculum leading to drastic increases in enrollments in college. "The number of students had jumped in the last decade of the nineteenth century from 156,756 to 237,592, and by 1910 was to rise to 355,213. By 1920 the enrollments had risen to 597,880" (DeVane, 1965, p. 15). This unfortunately was not the case for the reform movement in the 1960s.

Key takeaways AI generated

1. The 20th century marked the formalization of college majors from the elective system.
2. Enrollments rose dramatically from 156,756 in 1890 to 597,880 by 1920.
3. Prestigious institutions leveraged resources to attract scholars and donations, enhancing their status.
4. David Starr Jordan introduced the concept of a major subject at Indiana University in 1885.
5. The shift towards concentration and distribution requirements reflected faculty negotiations and institutional values.

FAQ's AI generated

What factors contributed to the rise of major concentrations in higher education? add

The paper reveals that by the early 20th century, influential leaders like David Starr Jordan at Indiana University initiated major subjects, leading to widespread adoption. Institutions like Yale and Harvard followed, refining their curricular structures to include specific major and general education requirements by 1909.

How did the elective system's decline influence curriculum development in universities? add

The study indicates that the decline of the elective system prompted colleges to adopt more structured curricula, focusing on concentrated subjects. By 1901, Yale began shifting towards concentration requirements, highlighting a broader movement away from flexibility in favor of academic coherence.

What role did faculty play in shaping general education requirements during the 20th century? add

The findings illustrate that faculty negotiations often influenced curriculum changes, especially regarding general education's breadth and distribution. This led to continual debates reflecting differing values among faculty about course design and curricular balance.

When did the concept of general education requirements emerge in U.S. colleges? add

General education requirements began surfacing around the turn of the century as colleges sought curricular reform. By 1905, Cornell was requiring distribution across specified knowledge areas, while similar frameworks emerged at other institutions soon after.

How did historical precedents shape the formation of majors in American higher education? add

The text notes that the tradition of focused studies stemmed from practices established in the late 19th century, like those at West Point and Rensselaer Polytechnic. This laid groundwork for later systematic approaches to major requirements in the early 20th century.
